property_summary: After any sequence of fallback calls with 10 ether, the difference between the current block timestamp and pastBlockTime must always be greater than 0 in the reference contract, but the mutant can set pastBlockTime equal to the current block timestamp within the same block.

After a successful fallback call, pastBlockTime must be strictly less than the current block timestamp in the reference contract, but the mutant can make them equal by allowing multiple calls in the same block.

After any sequence of successful fallback calls, the difference between the current block timestamp and pastBlockTime must always be greater than 0 in the reference, but the mutant allows them to be equal.

For any two successful fallback calls in the same block, the reference contract reverts the second call, breaking the property that `address(c).balance` never increases from a second call in the same block. The mutant allows both calls and can increase the balance, violating the invariant.

After a successful fallback call, the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime equal to the current block timestamp only if it was strictly less than the current block timestamp, so pastBlockTime is never updated more than once per block; the mutant can update pastBlockTime multiple times within the same block, changing the number of times block.number % 15 == 0 can trigger payouts.

After any successful fallback call, the value of pastBlockTime must be greater than or equal to the previous timestamp. The mutant sets pastBlockTime = block.timestamp and then the next call requires block.timestamp < pastBlockTime, which can never be true, making subsequent calls always revert.
After a successful fallback call, the contract's balance is zero; the buggy version permanently locks funds after the first call, so balance never becomes zero.

The fallback function must be callable again after a successful call; the reference allows subsequent calls, while the buggy version permanently reverts after the first call because it requires block.timestamp < pastBlockTime, which can never be true.

After any successful call to fallback (with exactly 10 ether and a block.timestamp increasing from the last call), the call must not revert; the reference allows subsequent calls as long as block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, while the buggy version requires a block.timestamp that can never be greater than the stored one, causing permanent reverts after the first successful call.

After any successful fallback call, a subsequent call is possible (i.e., does not revert) given a strictly increased block.timestamp; the reference allows it but the buggy version always reverts on the second attempt because it requires the impossible block.timestamp < pastBlockTime.
For any admissible call to fallback(), if msg.value was not exactly 10 ether, the call must revert; the buggy version allows such a call to succeed without reverting.
The fallback call must revert when msg.value is not exactly 10 ether, but the mutant allows such calls to succeed without reverting.
For any call to fallback(), if msg.value is not exactly 10 ether, the call must revert; the buggy version allows such calls to succeed (not revert) when block.timestamp > pastBlockTime.

After every successful fallback call, pastBlockTime must equal the timestamp of the block in which the call was executed; the mutant sets it to 0 instead, so any subsequent call in the same block or a later block will see a discrepancy.
After any sequence of valid fallback calls, pastBlockTime must equal the timestamp of the most recent call; the buggy version leaves it at 0, causing later calls to revert incorrectly.

After two consecutive valid fallback calls (each with 10 ether and strictly increasing block.timestamp), the pastBlockTime must eventually equal the timestamp of the second call; in the mutant, the second call reverts because pastBlockTime is never updated from the first call's timestamp, preventing any subsequent valid call.

After any valid fallback call, the contract's pastBlockTime must equal the block.timestamp of that call; the mutant fails to update it, so a subsequent call reverts even when all requirements are met.

For any sequence of fallback calls where only the first satisfies the checks and updates pastBlockTime, address(c).balance must equal the number of block.number%15==0 calls times 10 ether; the mutant never processes any call so balance stays 0, violating this relationship.
After a valid fallback call, pastBlockTime must be non-zero; the buggy version fails to update it, so it stays 0 and makes any subsequent valid call revert.

For any external call to fallback() with exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the contract's balance after the call must be zero if block.number is a multiple of 15, and equal to the pre-call balance plus 10 ether otherwise. The buggy version inverts this condition, causing the balance to be zero when block.number is NOT a multiple of 15.

For any valid call to fallback (exactly 10 ether, timestamp > pastBlockTime), the contract's balance afterward must be zero if and only if the block number is a multiple of 15; the buggy version inverts this, making the balance zero when block.number % 15 != 0 instead.
When block.number is divisible by 15, the sender's balance increases by exactly the full contract balance; the mutant violates this by transferring 0.

When the fallback is triggered and block.number is divisible by 15, the contract's entire balance must be transferred to the sender, leaving the contract with 0 balance; the mutant violates this by sending 0 instead.

After any interaction, pastBlockTime must equal the block.timestamp of the most recent previous interaction that updated it, so that the next call's require(block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) enforces strictly increasing timestamps; the buggy version updates pastBlockTime before the check, allowing the same block timestamp to pass the require.

When block.number ≤ 10, the reference allows fallback execution (subject to other requirements), but the buggy version always reverts due to the extra require, so the two versions differ in revert behavior for low blocks.

In the reference contract, a fallback call with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime always succeeds when block.number <= 10; the buggy version reverts for such calls, creating a revert-behavior divergence.
